Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 1–3:

﴿Ḥā Mīm. ʿAyn Sīn Qāf.﴾ The discussion of it is like that of the other letters of the alphabet (al-ḥurūf al-hijāʾiyya), as stated earlier in surah al-Baqara. Al-Ṭabarī reports that a man asked Ibn ʿAbbās about Ḥā Mīm ʿAyn Sīn Qāf, and he turned away from him. Then Ḥudhayfa said: Ibn ʿAbbās disliked it because it was revealed concerning a man from his family named ʿAbd Allāh, who builds a city on a river of the rivers of the East, and then Allah causes it to be swallowed up with its people at the end of time. The man, according to this, is Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr, and the city is Baghdad. It has been reported in a sound ḥadīth that it will be swallowed up.

﴿Thus does He reveal to you﴾: the kāf (thus) is an adjective (naʿt) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar), and the demonstrative "thus" refers to what the Qur'an or the surah contains. It has also been said that the reference is to His saying ﴿Ḥā Mīm. ʿAyn Sīn Qāf.﴾, for Allah revealed these very letters in every book He sent down. The soundness of this view is open to question.

﴿Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾: "Allah" is the subject (fāʿil) of yūḥī (He reveals). As for the reading ﴿yūḥā﴾ with a fatḥa, it is the subject (fāʿil) of a verb that is implied, which is indicated by yūḥī, as if someone had said: Who revealed it? So it was said: Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 5:

﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder﴾ meaning: they split apart out of fear of God and the greatness of His majesty. It was also said: out of the words of the disbelievers, "God has taken a son." This is like the verse in Maryam. Ibn 'Atiyya said: What the exegetes have stated here about weight and the like is rejected, because God, exalted is He, is not described by such things. ﴿from above them﴾: the pronoun refers to the heavens, and the meaning is that they split from their uppermost parts, which is an exaggeration in portraying the awesomeness. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the earths, but this is far-fetched. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, as if he said: from above the disbelieving groups, because of whose statements the heavens almost split apart; this too is far-fetched. ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those on the earth﴾: this is a general expression intended in a specific sense, because the angels only seek forgiveness for the believers among the people of the earth. It is like His saying: ﴿And they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. It was also said that the verse "and they seek forgiveness for those who believe" abrogates this verse, but this is false, because abrogation (naskh) does not apply to reports. It is possible that by seeking forgiveness is meant asking for forbearance toward the people of the earth, both believers and disbelievers, meaning: granting them respite and not hastening punishment against them, in which case it is general. If it is asked: what is the connection of His saying ﴿And the angels glorify the praises of their Lord﴾ with what precedes it? The answer: if we interpret the splitting of the heavens as arising from the greatness of God, then the angels' glorification is also an exaltation of Him, and the speech is coherent. If we interpret their splitting as arising from the disbelief of the children of Adam, then the angels' glorification is a declaration of God's transcendence above the disbelief of the children of Adam and their ugly statements.

Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Towns) is Makkah, and what is meant is its people. That is why it is followed by "and those around it" — meaning the people — "the Day of Assembly," meaning the Day of Resurrection, which is so named because all creatures will be gathered on it.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 42, verse 9:

﴿Or have they taken﴾ (am) is disjunctive (munqati'a), and "the protectors" (al-awliya') here means the deities worshipped besides Allah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 10:

﴿So its judgment rests with Allah﴾. That is, concerning whatever you and the disbelievers differ over regarding matters of religion, its judgment rests with Allah, by punishing the one who is in falsehood and rewarding the one who is in truth. Or, concerning whatever disputes you differ over, let them be brought for judgment before the Prophet (ﷺ), as in His saying: ﴿Then refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [An-Nisa: 59].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 11:

﴿مِّنْ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجاً﴾ means the females (al-inath). ﴿وَمِنَ ٱلأَنْعَامِ أَزْواجاً﴾ It is possible that it means the females, or the kinds (al-asnaf). ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ فِيهِ﴾ The meaning of yadhra'ukum is: He creates you as offspring after offspring and generation after generation. It was also said: He multiplies you. The pronoun in fihi refers to the making (al-ja'l) implied by His saying ﴿جَعَلَ لَكُم﴾. This is like when you say: "I spoke to Zayd a speech, in which I honored him." It was also said: the pronoun refers to marriage (al-tazwij), which is indicated by His saying ﴿أَزْوَاجاً﴾. Al-Zamakhshari said: its estimated meaning is ﴿يَذْرَؤُكُمْ﴾ "in this arrangement" (fi hadha al-tadbir), namely that He made people and livestock into pairs. The pronoun in yadhra'ukum is addressed to people, and in al-an'am (livestock) the rational ones are given precedence over the others. If it is asked: why did He say yadhra'ukum fihi and not yadhra'ukum bihi ("by it")? The answer: this arrangement was made like a source and a mine (al-manba' wa al-ma'din) for propagation and multiplication, as al-Zamakhshari said. ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ is a declaration of God the Exalted's transcendence above resembling created beings. Many people said: the kaf is extra (za'ida) for emphasis, and the meaning is "nothing is like Him." Al-Tabari and others said: it is not extra, but mithlihi has been placed in the position of huwa (He), and the meaning is "nothing is like He." Al-Zamakhshari said: this is like when you say: "One like you does not withhold," and what is meant is: "You do not withhold," so the withholding is negated from one like you, while what is meant is its negation from the essence itself.
[Ibn Juzayy's commentary on the words ﴿مَقَالِيدُ﴾ ("keys") in verse 42:12:] This has already been mentioned in Surah al-Zumar [39:63].

The religion of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) agrees with that of all the prophets in the fundamentals of belief, and this is what is meant here. That is why it is explained by His words: ﴿that you establish the religion﴾, meaning the establishment of Islam, which is the Oneness of God and obedience to Him, belief in His messengers, His books, and the Last Abode. As for the subsidiary legal rulings (al-ahkam al-far'iyya), the revealed laws (al-shara'i') differ concerning them, so they are not what is intended here. ﴿That you establish﴾ (أَنْ أَقِيمُواْ) may be in a position of accusative as a substitute for ﴿what He enjoined﴾ (مَا وَصَّىٰ), or in a position of genitive as a substitute for ﴿with it﴾ (بِهِ), or in a position of nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, or it may be an explanatory ʾan (مفسرة) with no place in the grammatical analysis (al-i'rab). ﴿What you call them to is grievous to the polytheists﴾ (كَبُرَ عَلَى ٱلْمُشْرِكِينَ مَا تَدْعُوهُمْ إِلَيْهِ), meaning Islam was difficult for the polytheists. ﴿God chooses whom He wills﴾ (ٱللَّهُ يَجْتَبِيۤ إِلَيْهِ مَن يَشَآءُ). The pronoun in إليه refers to God Most High, and it has been said that it refers to the religion.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 14:

﴿وَمَا تَفَرَّقُوا﴾ meaning: the people of the different religions, from the Jews and the Christians and others. ﴿وَلَوْلَا كَلِمَةٌ﴾ meaning: the previous decree that they would not be judged between in this world. ﴿وَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ أُورِثُوا الْكِتَابَ﴾ meaning: the contemporaries of our master Muhammad (ﷺ) from the Jews and the Christians. It is also said: meaning the Arabs, and the Book, according to this, is the Qur'an. ﴿لَفِي شَكٍّ مِّنْهُ﴾ The pronoun refers to the Book, or to the religion, or to our master Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 15:

﴿So for that [reason], invite [them]﴾ i.e., to that which Allah has prescribed. So invite people; the lam here means "to" (ila). The demonstrative "that" refers either to His saying "He has prescribed for you of the religion" or to His saying "that to which you invite them." It is also said that the lam means "because of" (ajl), and the demonstrative refers to the division and disagreement; that is, because of the division that has occurred, invite to Allah. On this view, His saying "and be steadfast" is conjoined (ma'tuf), whereas on the first view it is a new sentence (mustaʼnaf), so one stops at ﴿invite and be steadfast﴾.

﴿as you have been commanded﴾ i.e., remain upon what you have been commanded: worshipping Allah, obeying Him, and conveying His message.

﴿And do not follow their desires﴾ The pronoun in "their" refers to the disbelievers. Their desires are what they loved of disbelief and falsehood in its entirety.

﴿And say: "I have been commanded to act justly among you"﴾ It is said: this means justice in judgments when they bring their disputes before him. It may also mean justice in calling them to the religion of Islam, i.e., I have been commanded to lead you to the truth.

﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾ i.e., there is no disputation or debate, for the truth has become manifest, and you are being obstinate.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 16:

﴿And those who argue about God﴾ means: who dispute with the believers concerning the religion of Islam. It refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, and it has been said: to the Jews. ﴿after it has been responded to﴾ The pronoun refers to God, meaning: after people have responded to Him and entered His religion. It has been said that it refers to the religion, and it has been said that it refers to Muhammad ﷺ. The first view is the most apparent and the best. ﴿their argument is baseless﴾ meaning: vanished, false.

Revealed the Book (ﷺ) (ﷺ)... 

Let me translate carefully.

**"It is Allah who has revealed the Book"**, meaning the genus of the Book, **"with the truth"**, i.e., with what is binding, or containing the truth, **"and the Balance"**. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: it means justice (ʿadl). The meaning of sending down justice is sending down the command to it in the revealed Books. It was also said: it means the well-known balance (mīzān). If it is asked: what is the connection between the mention of the Book and the Balance and the mention of the Hour? The answer is that the Hour is the Day of recompense and reckoning, so it is as if He said: be just and do what is right before the Day on which you will be called to account for your deeds. **"And what will make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near"**, [the verb] came as *qarīb* in the masculine, because the feminine of *al-sāʿa* (the Hour) is not real (ḥaqīqī), and because what is meant by it is the time of the Hour.

﴿They seek to hasten it﴾: that is, they ask for it to be brought quickly, mocking it and seeking to discredit the believers. ﴿They dispute about it﴾: that is, they argue and oppose.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 19:

﴿He provides for whom He wills﴿ means: the provision beyond what is guaranteed for every living creature, as in His saying: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ [Hud: 6], that is, what sustains life. This applies generally to every living creature throughout its lifetime, while the surplus is specific to whomever Allah wills.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 20:

﴿The tilth of the Hereafter﴾ is an expression for working for it, and likewise the tilth of this world, and it is borrowed from the tilling of the land, because the farmer works and awaits the benefit of what he has done. ﴿We increase for him in his tilth﴾ is an expression for multiplying the reward. ﴿We give him of it﴾, that is, We give him of it what has been decreed for him, because every person must receive what has been apportioned to him. ﴿And he has no share in the Hereafter﴾: this is for the disbelievers, or for one who desires only the worldly life and has no desire for the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 21:

﴿Am lahum﴾ "Am" is here munqati'a (disjunctive), used for denunciation and reproach. The "shuraka'" (partners) are the idols and others; it is also said they are the devils. ﴿Shara'u lahum min al-din ma lam ya'dh bihi Allah﴾ The pronoun in "shara'u" refers to the partners, and the pronoun in "lahum" refers to the disbelievers; it is also said the reverse is the case, and the first is more apparent. ﴿Lam ya'dh﴾ means: did not command. What is meant by "what they legislated" is the falsehoods in beliefs and in actions, such as the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and left unridden), the wasila (a she-camel or sheep released for its owners' idols), and other such things.

﴿Wa-lawla kalimat al-fasl﴾ That is: were it not for the prior decree that they would not be judged between in this world, they would have been judged between in it.
﴿You will see the wrongdoers fearful﴾ — meaning, in the Hereafter.

That is the one which Allah gives good tidings of to His servants. [Its] estimated meaning is "gives good tidings of it," and the preposition with its object has been omitted. ﴿Except affection toward the near kin.﴾ On this there are four opinions. The first: that "al-qurba" means "al-qarabah" (kinship), and "fi" means "min ajl" (for the sake of). The meaning is: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except that you love me for the sake of the kinship between me and you." So the aim on this view is to win the sympathy of Quraysh, and there was no clan among them without some kinship between it and the Prophet ﷺ. The second: that "al-qurba" means "al-aqarib" (relatives), or "dhu al-qurba" (kinsfolk). The meaning is: "except that you love my relatives and protect me through them." The aim on this view is an injunction concerning the Family of the House (Ahl al-Bayt). The third: that "al-qurba" is the kinship of people with one another. The meaning is that you love your own relatives, and the aim on this view is an injunction to maintain the ties of kinship (silat al-arham). The fourth: that "al-qurba" is drawing near to Allah, and the meaning is: "except that you draw near to Allah by obeying Him." The exception is disjunctive (munqati') on the third and fourth opinions. As for the first and second, it may be disjunctive, because affection is not a wage, and it may be connected (muttasil) in a figurative sense, as if he had said: "I do not ask you for any reward for it, except affection," thus treating affection as if it were the wage. ﴿Whoever commits a good deed (yaqtarif)﴾ means "yaktasib" (earns), ﴿We increase for him therein good (husn)﴾ means the multiplication of reward.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 24:

﴿Am yaqooloona﴾ (Am yaqūlūn): "am" is here disjunctive (munqati'ah), used for denial and rebuke. ﴿If Allah wills, He would seal over your heart﴾ — regarding the meaning of this, there are two opinions. The first is that it is a reply to the disbelievers in their saying, "He has invented a lie against Allah." That is: had you invented a lie against Allah, He would have sealed over your heart; but you did not invent a lie against Allah, so He guided you and kept you firm. The second is that the intended meaning is: if Allah wills, He would seal over your heart through patience in the face of the disbelievers' words and bearing their harm. ﴿And Allah effaces falsehood﴾ — this is a new verb (fi'l mustani'af), not conjoined to what precedes it, because the preceding verb is in the jussive (majzum) while this one is in the indicative (marfu'), so it is pausing upon what precedes and beginning with this. Regarding its meaning there are two views. The first is that it is a continuation of what precedes: that is, had you invented a lie against Allah, He would have sealed over your heart and effaced the falsehood you would have been inventing, had you invented it. The second is that it is a promise to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that Allah will efface falsehood, which is disbelief, and establish the truth, which is Islam.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verses 25–26:

﴿And He it is who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ ﴿"ʿan" (عَنْ) here means "min" (from)﴾, as if He said: the repentance issuing from His servants. Acceptance of repentance is of three kinds. The first is repentance from disbelief, which is certainly accepted. The second is repentance from wrongs done to people, which is not accepted until the wrongs are returned or the wronged party's forgiveness is obtained. The third is repentance from sins between the servant and Allah. The sound view is that these are accepted, by the evidence of this verse. It was also said that they are subject to His will.

﴿And pardons the evil deeds﴾. Pardon together with repentance follows what we have mentioned. As for pardon without repentance, it is of four kinds. The first is pardon of disbelief, which does not occur at all. The second is pardon of wrongs done to people, which is likewise. The third is pardon of minor sins when major sins are avoided, which is agreed upon. The fourth is pardon of major sins. The position of the People of the Sunnah is that they are subject to His will, while the position of the Mu'tazilah is that they are not forgiven except through repentance.

﴿And responds to those who believe﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first is that the meaning of "yastajību" is "yujību" (responds), with "alladhīna āmanū" (those who believe) as the object, and the subject is a pronoun referring to Allah, Exalted is He, meaning He responds to them in what they ask of Him. Al-Zamakhshari said: its original form is "yastajību li-lladhīna āmanū," so the lam was omitted. The second is that it means "yujību," with "alladhīna āmanū" as the subject, meaning the believers respond to their Lord by following His religion. The third is that it means the believers seek a response from their Lord, the form "istafʿala" here being on its usual pattern of seeking. The first is the more preferred, due to the indication of His saying: ﴿and increases them from His bounty﴾; and because it is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Muʿadh ibn Jabal.

﴿And increases them from His bounty﴾, meaning He grants them what they did not ask for, in addition to responding to what they asked. This increase has been narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) as being intercession and good pleasure.

Ibn Juzayy, *al-Tashil*, on Surah 42, verse 27:

﴿If God were to expand provision for His servants, they would surely rebel in the earth.﴾ That is, some of them would transgress against others and become insolent, because wealth brings about insolence. Some of the Companions (ṣaḥābah) said: "It was revealed concerning us, for we looked at the wealth of the disbelievers and longed for it."

﴿And it is He who sends down the rain after they have despaired﴾. It was said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him: "The drought has grown severe and the people have despaired." He said: "Now they will receive rain," and he took this from this verse. From the same source is his ﷺ saying: "Intensify, O hardship, so that you may be relieved." ﴿And He spreads His mercy﴾. It was said: it means the rain, so this is a repetition of the first meaning in different words. It was also said: it means the sun. And it was said: it is general.

And He spreads throughout them both every creature (﴿وَمَا بَثَّ فِيهِمَا مِن دَآبَّةٍ﴾). There is no difficulty here, since the creatures (dawab) are on the earth. As for the heavens, it is said: it means the angels. It is also said: it is possible that there are creatures in the heavens which we do not know. It is also said: the meaning is that He spread them in one of the two, and so mentioned the two, just as you say "the sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when it was only in some of them. ﴿وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ جَمْعِهِمْ إِذَا يَشَآءُ قَدِيرٌ﴾ And He is Able to gather them whenever He wills (﴿وَهُوَ عَلَىٰ جَمْعِهِمْ إِذَا يَشَآءُ قَدِيرٌ﴾). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 30:

There are two views on this. The first is that it is an expression for humiliation, because the gaze of the humiliated person is one of awe and submission. The second is that they will be gathered blind, so they do not look with their eyes but look with their hearts. Ibn 'Atiyyah and al-Zamakhshari considered this unlikely. The phrase "from a hidden glance" may mean the eye, or it may be a verbal noun (*masdar*). ﴿On the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected either to "He will say" or to "they have lost." ﴿Unquestionably, the wrongdoers﴾: this may be part of the speech of those who believed, or it may be a fresh statement from the speech of Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 47:

﴿There is no repelling it﴾. This was mentioned in Ghafir [40:11]. ﴿from any denial﴾, meaning: any denial; that is, you will not be able to deny your deeds.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 49:

﴿He bestows females upon whom He wills﴾. He placed the females first, showing care for them and giving comfort to the one to whom they are granted. Wathila ibn al-Asqa' said: "Among the blessings of a woman is that she bears a female first, before a male, because Allah began with the females."

Some of them said: this verse was revealed concerning the prophets, peace be upon them. Shu'ayb and Lut had females without males, Ibrahim had males without females, Muhammad (ﷺ) had both females and males, and Yahya was barren. The apparent meaning is that it is general for all people, since each one of them is not free of one of these four categories that were mentioned. In the verse there is also, among the tools of exposition, the device of division (al-taqsim).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 51:

﴿And it is not for a human being that Allah should speak to him except by revelation﴾ – the verse. In it Allah, exalted is He, explains His speech to His servants, and He made it in three modes. The first is the one mentioned first, which occurs by inspiration (ilham) or in a dream. The second is that he hears His speech from behind a veil. The third is revelation through the intermediary of the angel, and this is His saying: ﴿or sends a messenger﴾, meaning an angel, who then reveals by His permission whatever He wills to the Prophet. This third mode is specific to the prophets. The second is specific to Musa (Moses) and to Muhammad (ﷺ), since Allah spoke to him on the night of the Isra' (Night Journey). As for the first, it occurs frequently for the prophets and the saints (awliya'), and it may occur for all of creation, and among it is: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾ [al-Nahl: 68], and among it are people's dreams. ﴿or sends a messenger﴾: Nafi' read "yursila" and "yuhiya" with a raised vowel (raf'), on the assumption of the sense "or He [himself] sends," while the rest read them in the accusative (nasb), coordinating them with "wahyan" (revelation), because its implied sense is "an yuhiya," coordinated with the implied "an" (that).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 42, verse 52:

﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit (rūḥan) from Our command.﴾ Here "the spirit" (al-rūḥ) means the Qur'an. The meaning is: like this revelation, by sending an angel, We revealed the Qur'an to you. "Command" (al-amr) here may be understood as the singular of "affairs" (al-umūr), or it may be taken from the sense of commanding something.

﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was.﴾ The purpose of this statement is two things. The first is to enumerate the blessing upon him (ﷺ), that Allah taught him what he had not known. The second is an argument for his prophethood, since he brought what he did not know and what no one had taught him. If it is said: as for his not knowing the Book, there is no difficulty in that, but as for faith (al-īmān), there is a difficulty, because the prophets are believers in Allah before their mission? The answer is that faith (al-īmān) comprises many kinds of knowledge, and he only came to perfect knowledge of them after his commissioning, although he was already a believer in Allah before that. So "faith" here means the perfection of knowledge, which he attained through prophethood.

﴿But We made it a light.﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an.
